questions.question: Two point charges $q_1 = 3\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and $q_2 = 5\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ are separated by $r = 0.3\ \mathrm{m}$. Find the electrostatic force between them. Is it attractive or repulsive? Use $k = 9\times10^9\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2}$.
questions.answer:
$F = k\dfrac{|q_1||q_2|}{r^2} = 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{3\times10^{-6} \times 5\times10^{-6}}{(0.3)^2}$

$= 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{15\times10^{-12}}{0.09} = 9\times10^9 \times 1.667\times10^{-10} = 1.5\ \mathrm{N}$

Both charges are positive $\Rightarrow$ **repulsive** force.

questions.question: A point charge $q = 2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ creates an electric field. Find the field magnitude at $r = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ from the charge. Use $k = 9\times10^9\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2}$.
Two charges $q_1 = +4\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and $q_2 = -4\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ are placed $d = 0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the electric field at the midpoint between them.
questions.answer:
At the midpoint, $r = d/2 = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}$ from each charge.

$E_1 = k\dfrac{q_1}{r^2} = 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{4\times10^{-6}}{0.01} = 3.6\times10^6\ \mathrm{N/C}$, pointing **away** from $+q_1$ (toward $-q_2$)

$E_2 = k\dfrac{|q_2|}{r^2} = 3.6\times10^6\ \mathrm{N/C}$, pointing **toward** $-q_2$ (same direction!)

Both fields point in the **same direction** (from $+$ to $-$):

$E = E_1 + E_2 = 7.2\times10^6\ \mathrm{N/C}$ (pointing from $q_1$ toward $q_2$)

questions.question: Find the electrostatic potential energy of a system of two charges $q_1 = 2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and $q_2 = -3\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ separated by $r = 0.4\ \mathrm{m}$.
questions.answer:
$U = k\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r} = 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{(2\times10^{-6})(-3\times10^{-6})}{0.4}$

$= 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{-6\times10^{-12}}{0.4} = 9\times10^9 \times (-1.5\times10^{-11})$

$= -0.135\ \mathrm{J}$

Negative potential energy indicates the charges attract each other (bound system).

questions.question: Three equal charges $q = 1\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle with side $a = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}$. Find: (a) the net force on one charge, (b) the total potential energy of the system.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Force from each of the other two charges:

$F = k\dfrac{q^2}{a^2} = 9\times10^9 \times \dfrac{10^{-12}}{0.01} = 0.9\ \mathrm{N}$

These forces are at $60°$ to each other (by symmetry, the triangle gives $60°$ between them). By vector addition:

$|F_{\text{net}}| = 2F\cos(30°) = 2 \times 0.9 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.9\sqrt{3} \approx 1.56\ \mathrm{N}$ (pointing outward from the centroid)

**(b)** There are 3 pairs, each with $U = kq^2/a$:

$U_{\text{total}} = 3 \times \dfrac{kq^2}{a} = 3 \times \dfrac{9\times10^9 \times 10^{-12}}{0.1} = 3 \times 0.09 = 0.27\ \mathrm{J}$

questions.question: Charge $q_1 = +6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ is at the origin. Charge $q_2 = -2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ is at $x = 0.4\ \mathrm{m}$. Find the point on the $x$-axis (excluding between the charges) where the net electric field is zero.
questions.answer:
Outside the segment, the zero-field point is on the side of the smaller magnitude charge (to the right of $q_2$).

At position $x > 0.4\ \mathrm{m}$, let $x$ be the distance from origin:

$E_1 = k\dfrac{6}{x^2}$ (rightward, away from $+q_1$)

$E_2 = k\dfrac{2}{(x-0.4)^2}$ (leftward, toward $-q_2$)

Set equal: $\dfrac{6}{x^2} = \dfrac{2}{(x-0.4)^2}$

$3(x-0.4)^2 = x^2$

$\sqrt{3}(x-0.4) = x$ (taking positive root)

$(\sqrt{3}-1)x = 0.4\sqrt{3}$

$x = \dfrac{0.4\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}-1} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.732} \approx 0.946\ \mathrm{m}$

questions.question: A charge $q = -5\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ is moved from a point where $V_A = 200\ \mathrm{V}$ to a point where $V_B = 800\ \mathrm{V}$. Find the work done by the electric force.
questions.answer:
Work done by the electric force:

$W = q(V_A - V_B) = (-5\times10^{-6})(200 - 800) = (-5\times10^{-6})(-600) = 3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J} = 3\ \mathrm{mJ}$

Positive work done by electric force on the negative charge moving to higher potential — consistent with the fact that negative charges move naturally toward higher potential.

questions.question: Two point charges $q_1 = +q$ and $q_2 = -q$ are separated by distance $2d$. Find the electric potential at the midpoint between them.
questions.answer:
At the midpoint, the distance to each charge is $d$.

$V = V_1 + V_2 = k\dfrac{q}{d} + k\dfrac{-q}{d} = k\dfrac{q}{d} - k\dfrac{q}{d} = 0$

The electric **potential** is zero at the midpoint, but the electric **field** is not zero (it points from $+q$ toward $-q$ and both fields add).

questions.question: An electron ($q = -1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $m = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$) is accelerated through a potential difference of $\Delta V = 100\ \mathrm{V}$. Find its final speed (starting from rest).
questions.answer:
Work-energy theorem: $q\Delta V = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$

The electron gains kinetic energy equal to $|q|\Delta V$ (since $q < 0$ and $\Delta V$ is applied to accelerate it):

$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = |q|\Delta V = 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 100 = 1.6\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{J}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6\times10^{-17}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}} = \sqrt{3.513\times10^{13}} \approx 5.93\times10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}$

questions.question: Show that the electric potential energy of two point charges can be written as $U = kq_1q_2/r$, starting from the work done to bring $q_2$ from infinity to distance $r$ from $q_1$.
questions.answer:
Start with $q_1$ fixed at the origin. The force on test charge $q_2$ at position $r'$ is:

$F = k\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r'^2}$ (along $\hat{r}$)

Work done by electric force to bring $q_2$ from $\infty$ to $r$:

$W = \int_\infty^r F\,dr' = \int_\infty^r k\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r'^2}\,dr'$

$= kq_1q_2 \left[-\dfrac{1}{r'}\right]_\infty^r = kq_1q_2\left(-\dfrac{1}{r} + 0\right) = -\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}$

Potential energy = $-W$ (= work done **against** the force):

$$U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}$$

For like charges ($q_1q_2 > 0$): $U > 0$ (repulsive, need to do work to bring them together)
For unlike charges ($q_1q_2 < 0$): $U < 0$ (attractive, energy is released)
